    DIY Guide: Maximalist Caribbean Mystic Jewelry & Belts

    A sourcing, fabrication, and styling field guide — raw brass, cowrie, sea glass, bush seed, and the collected-not-coordinated mantra

    nyaamye · Companion to the Loc Adornment Compendium

    The Caribbean aesthetic is a living archive—a dense, multi-layered tapestry woven from indigenous roots, African spiritual traditions, South Asian diaspora histories, and maritime trade. Embracing a maximalist "Caribbean Mystic" look means moving past commercial souvenir trinkets and leaning into heavy textures, antique metals, organic shore elements, and intentional hand-crafting.

    1. DIY Sourcing & Manufacturing Strategy

    Creating bespoke, heirloom-quality maximalist jewelry requires sourcing raw, authentic materials in bulk and mastering foundational assembly methods.

    Core Materials & Sourcing Matrix

    Glass Seed Beads (Czech/Miyuki, 6/0 & 8/0)

    Avoid plastic beads. Sourcing heavy glass beads ensures proper drape, weight, and light refraction. Look for opaque terra cotta, deep cobalt, metallic gold, and milky white shades.

    Ghanaian Permanent Thread & Cordage

    Utilize bonded nylon or traditional Ghanaian cotton/poly bead thread (often used for waist beads). It is rot-resistant, waterproof, and holds firm under high tension.

    Pre-Drilled Cowrie Shells (Cypraea moneta)

    Purchase bulk natural cowries with sliced backs or pre-drilled holes. Ensure shells are ethically harvested and unbleached for organic color variation.

    Bulk Brass Ghungroo Bells & Coins

    Source raw, unpolished Indian brass ghungroo bells and stamped alloy coin charms. The raw brass will naturally oxidize with skin contact and sea air, developing a rich patina.

    Wire & Findings

    Stock 18-gauge and 20-gauge raw brass wire for heavy wraps, along with heavy-duty jump rings (8mm–10mm, 1.2mm thickness) to prevent structural failure.

    Wire-Wrapping & Fabrication Techniques

    The Briolette & Raw Stone Wrap
    Pass a 20-gauge brass wire through a sea glass or stone perforation. Bend both ends upward at 90-degree angles to cross above the stone. Wrap the shorter tail around the longer stem 3 times, form a top loop with round-nose pliers, and wrap the remaining tail downward to lock the core.
    Upcycling & Thrifting Salvage
    Hunt for vintage leather belts, broken brass chandeliers, multi-strand costume necklaces, and solid brass keys at estate sales. Deconstruct factory-made jewelry to harvest heavy clasps, filigree connectors, and base chains, then integrate them with organic elements.

    2. Waist Belts & Low-Rise Styling

    Low-rise silhouettes—such as utility cargos, distressed denim, and tiered linen skirts—serve as the canvas for heavy, multi-layered waist adornment.

    Construction Architecture: Coin, Temple & Waist Belts

    To build a balanced, structural low-rise waist chain system, follow a three-tier construction process:

    1

    Base Anchor Layer Structural

    A 1.5-inch wide vegetable-tanned leather strip or heavy braided cotton cord equipped with a double-ring brass buckle. This anchors the weight across the high hips.

    2

    Mid-Weight Kinetic Layer Sound & Movement

    A secondary chain composed of interconnected 10mm brass jump rings, strand-strung cowrie shells, and hanging brass coins. Space coins 1.5 inches apart to allow free movement without tangling.

    3

    Dangling Fringe Layer Tactile & Visual

    Clusters of brass ghungroo bells affixed to 2-inch chain drops, intermingled with heavy raw glass beads.

    Base Anchor Layer — Braided Leather / Heavy Cord
    Mid-Layer — Interconnected Brass Chain & Cowrie Shells
    ○   ○   ○     ○   ○   ○     ○   ○   ○   (Ghungroos)

    Layering Over Garments

    Over Cargo Pants
    Sling a heavy brass coin belt low on the hips, resting right below the waistband. Let the ghungroo drops spill over the cargo side pockets to contrast utilitarian canvas with fluid metallic movement.
    Over Tiered Maxi Skirts
    Combine a thick woven hemp belt with two asymmetrical waist beads that drop diagonally across the pelvis, tucking one side slightly under the waistband for an effortless, gathered drape.

    3. Integrating Indian & Temple Jewelry

    The Caribbean aesthetic is deeply shaped by Indo-Caribbean heritage, stemming from the post-emancipation arrival of indentured laborers from Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Tamil Nadu. This cultural synthesis infused the region's style with rich metalworking, coin ornamentations, and protective talismanic motifs.

    The “Collected, Not Coordinated” Mantra

    Avoid matching sets. The Caribbean Mystic aesthetic relies on an accumulation of personal history, trade, and memory. Combine dark oxidized silvers with rich antique golds, balancing ornate craftsmanship with raw, unpolished elements.

    Collected, Not Coordinated
    Raw / Organic ElementsAntique Metal / Sculptural
    Freeform locs or textured hair twistsAntique gold-plated Kadas
    Uncut sea glass bound in raw brassTemple pendants (Lakshmi)
    Driftwood beads & wild Job’s Tears bush seedsHeavy chokers with coins

    Styling High-Contrast Pieces

    Heavy Kadas & Raw Wrists
    Stack thick, carved brass Indian kadas (rigid bangles) alongside simple hand-braided hemp cords and worn leather cuffs.
    Temple Pendants & Organic Textures
    Nest ornate temple pendants depicting deities or flora against raw, freeform locs, coils, or deep-textured linen wraps. Position the metallic focal point directly against bare skin or simple, unembellished fabrics.

    4. Island Roots & Materiality

    Authentic Caribbean maximalism is tied to materiality—drawing directly from island ecology, geological history, and coastal gathering.

    🐚 Coastal Shells

    Conch FragmentsSmooth Sea GlassBleached Coral Spines

    🌰 Botanic Seeds

    Job’s TearsOrmosia (Red/Black)Tamarind Seeds

    🪵 Wood & Bark

    Carved Lignum VitaeDriftwood BeadsMahogany Cabochons

    Regional Material Culture: St. Vincent & Tortola

    St. Vincent (Yurumein)
    Renowned for black sand volcanic geology, dark river stones, and rich native woods. Incorporate polished black river stones wire-wrapped in raw copper, alongside carved mahogany or Lignum Vitae (Tree of Life) accents.
    Tortola & Virgin Islands
    Defined by turquoise coastal shelf waters, reef formations, and maritime sea-faring influences. Focus on naturally tumbled sea glass (cobalt, olive, and amber), smooth conch shell fragments, and bleached coral spines.

    Building an Authentic Personal Archive

    Replace commercial plastic souvenir beads with items sourced through direct collection and intentional trade:

    Foraged Bush Seeds
    Harvest Coix lacryma-jobi (Job’s Tears) or Ormosia (Jump-Up/Red-and-Black) seeds. Pierce them with a heated needle, then seal them with natural oils before stringing.
    Shoreline Treasures
    Drill small holes through thick conch lip fragments using diamond-tipped drill bits under water. Pair them with tumbled sea glass held in place by low-profile wire cages.

    5. Smart Buying Filter

    Not everything should be made at home. Heavy casting, structural metalwork, and intricate lapidary work require specialized tools, whereas assembly, stringing, and wrapping are ideal for DIY projects.

    Field Checklist for the Caribbean Mystic Maker

    Test Thread Integrity
    Always perform a hard tension pull test on bonded nylon thread before stringing heavy brass or glass beads.
    Mix Patinas
    Do not polish away tarnish on vintage brass or silver; the dark oxidation provides necessary contrast against bright shells and polished glass.
    Sound Matters
    Pay attention to the acoustic profile of your pieces. The combination of brass ghungroo bells and clinking cowrie shells creates a subtle, melodic chime with every step.

    🌿🕯️

    Bush Girl Medicine School

    A Future Roadmap — Not an Active Task List

    Companion to The Root Below the Root — where the research could eventually go, once the current reading is actually finished

    This document exists so the full scope of this vision has a real home — without turning every reading session into a 40-subject syllabus. Nothing here is due. Nothing here is required before you're "allowed" to practice. This is a map, not a checklist. The active working document (The Root Below the Root) stays focused on St. Vincent, Tortola, and the three books currently in hand.

    🧭 The Core Reframe

    Not: "prove whether my ancestors practiced Obeah." Instead: become someone who can recognize what my ancestors left me, what history erased, what the land still teaches, and what I must never pretend to know.

    You do not need to prove Akan ancestry before you're allowed to learn. You don't need a family member to hand you a tradition for the work to be meaningful. What you need is a rigorous way of separating: what ancestors may have carried → what survived in SVG/BVI → what Obeah actually means historically → what Shaker/Converted practice preserved → what Akan traditions actually teach → what you personally experience → what you choose to practice today.

    🌗 The 16 Branches

    The organizing architecture. Each branch below folds in the specific study areas from the original 40-item list.

    🌿 LAND

    • Ethnobotany — not "this plant is good for X," but which part is used, when harvested, who traditionally gathers it, food vs. medicine, physical vs. spiritual medicine, which plants are African/Indigenous/European in origin
    • Botany (species-level identification), pharmacognosy, toxicology, herb-drug interactions, dosage/preparation forms (tea ≠ tincture ≠ decoction ≠ poultice), maternal/infant safety, plant conservation
    • Provision grounds, enslaved people's gardens, seed saving, planting cycles, wild harvesting, food sovereignty
    • Weather and environmental signs (clouds, wind, thunder, tides, hurricanes) — held separately from spiritual interpretation of them

    A THE BUSH GIRL MATERIA MEDICA record for each plant: local name, scientific name, SVG/BVI name, other Caribbean names, part used, preparation, traditional purpose, documented Caribbean use, African parallels, Indigenous parallels, food use, spiritual/ritual association, toxicity/contraindications, pregnancy/child safety, evidence level, personal experience.

    🫀 BODY

    • Hair, nails, blood, saliva, breath, sweat, feet, hands, menstrual substances historically, pregnancy/birth, bathing, washing, clothing, bodily boundaries — not assuming every tradition treats these the same way
    • Reproductive knowledge as its own category: fertility, pregnancy, childbirth, midwifery, postpartum care, breastfeeding, infant protection, miscarriage, naming, baptism, mother-child spiritual bonds

    🌊 WATER

    • Rivers, springs, sea, beaches, freshwater vs. saltwater, cleansing, life/death associations
    • The sea as its own discipline for a Tortola/St. Vincent practitioner: fishing, tides, currents, storms, maritime trade, water spirits, drowning/death at sea, coastal plants, islands as connected rather than isolated

    🔥 POWER

    • THE SHADOW SIDE — curses, hexes, spiritual attack, "sending" illness/misfortune, poisoning vs. spiritual affliction, binding, crossing, spiritual contamination, offended spirits, broken taboos, revenge workings — studied as: what did the community believe was happening, who was believed capable, how did people respond? Not treated as an objectively-supernatural-events log
    • The dangerous side of the healer: healer → protector → diviner → mediator → feared person are not separate categories. Why did communities fear the same people they depended on?
    • Protection: spiritual cleansing, protective prayers/objects, thresholds and boundaries, water, smoke/incense, salt, iron/metal, household protections, graveyard/death protections, divination as danger-identification
    • Poisoning vs. "obeah" as its own research module — the boundary between medicine, herbalism, poison, witchcraft, spiritual healing, and spiritual attack was historically blurred, partly for colonial reasons. Core question: when historical records say "obeah," what were they actually describing?
    • Counter-magic/reversal: what did people do when they believed something had already been done to them? Reversal, uncrossing, cleansing, identifying the alleged source, communal intervention — historical systems, not a how-to manual

    Formal principle: knowing that something exists does not obligate practicing it. Historical knowledge, practitioner knowledge, and personal revelation are legitimate areas of study. Operational "exactly how do I make this happen" — especially involving poisoning, physical harm, or coercion — is where real boundaries belong.

    🕯️ SPIRIT

    • Cosmology as the map underneath everything: what is God/the Creator, what are spirits, what are ancestors, are ancestors still active, what is the soul, can spirits inhabit places/objects/animals/water/trees, what happens after death, origin of illness and evil, how Christian and African-derived cosmologies merge
    • "The Dead Are Not Automatically Harmless": which spirits were benevolent vs. dangerous, what made a dead person become troublesome, why certain mourning nights mattered, what protected the living, what happened after violent/unnatural death — SVG-specific evidence first, never imported wholesale from Haiti/Jamaica/Ghana/Trinidad/Yoruba tradition

    👁️ KNOWING

    • Divination as its own discipline: dreams, omens, signs, second sight, prophetic experience, divining causes of illness/misfortune, discernment ("is this spiritual, physical, psychological, social, or coincidence?"), who historically had authority to interpret signs
    • Spiritual diagnosis: the range of explanations for illness/misfortune/nightmares/bad luck — physical, environmental, interpersonal, moral/spiritual, ancestor issues, witchcraft, or coincidence. The skill is not jumping to the most supernatural explanation first
    • Dreams and altered states in depth: prophetic dreams, visitation dreams, grief dreams, possession, trance, ecstatic prayer, shaking, visions, spiritual travel, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic experience — and how different frameworks interpret the same experience differently

    ⚖️ LAW

    • Taboo and prohibition: things not to do/say, places not to enter, timing restrictions, food restrictions, treatment of sacred objects and the dead, consequences of violation. Sometimes the most important part of a tradition is not the ritual — it's under what circumstances you must NOT do it
    • Initiation, apprenticeship, and authority: how someone historically became a healer/spiritual worker, whether knowledge was inherited/revealed/taught/purchased/earned/initiated, what separated a legitimate practitioner from a fraud, what can be self-studied vs. what belonged to an initiated/community context

    🪶 PEOPLE

    • Women's knowledge as a major category: midwives, herbalists, wet nurses, mourners, spiritual workers, dream interpreters, market women, elderly and disabled women's medical labor — historically domestic, not institutional, and therefore easily erased from archives
    • Gender and power more broadly: what could women do that men couldn't and vice versa, who was feared/trusted/accused/punished, how colonial gender structures changed these roles
    • Healing institutions: who actually cared for sick people — enslaved healers, midwives, bush doctors, spiritual workers, physicians, plantation medical systems — and the conflicts between them
    • Childhood and initiation into knowledge: when and what children were traditionally taught about plants, graves, water, spirits, danger, death

    🥁 VOICE

    • Especially relevant to the Shaker/Spiritual Baptist branch: shouting, singing, call-and-response, drumming, bells, clapping, dancing, trembling/shaking, possession, altered states, breath, silence, prayer, repetitive speech — what the body does when someone enters a religious/spiritual state
    • Music as historical evidence: Bamboula, fungi, camfou/comfoo, Big Drum, Shaker music, work songs, wake singing — with African linguistic origins for BVI-specific terms held as proposed, not confirmed, until independently verified
    • Sound archives and oral history: old recordings, sermons, hymns, storytelling, proverbs, work songs — what information is encoded in performance itself (accent, rhythm, repetition, gesture), especially valuable given no family interview access

    🾤 OBJECTS

    • Sacred/material culture: bottles, jars, bowls, candles, cloth, beads, shells, bells, iron, water vessels, roots, stones, crosses, Bibles, grave objects. For each: what did it mean, who handled it, where was it placed, why that material
    • Material archaeology beneath written history: plantation archaeology, enslaved settlements, domestic objects, pottery, tools, botanical remains, burial grounds, hidden spaces

    🗺️ PLACE

    • Sacred geography: rivers, springs, sea, beaches, caves, mountains, crossroads, forests, old houses, graves, boundaries, wells, specific trees — and whether SVG, Tortola, and the wider Virgin Islands have documented place-specific spiritual geographies
    • Time and spiritual timing as its own category: days of the week, dawn/dusk, moon phases, rainy/dry seasons, death anniversaries, 3rd/9th/40th days, feast days, All Saints/All Souls — checked for what's actually documented in SVG/BVI specifically vs. imported from elsewhere
    • Numbers and patterns: investigated for documented significance in SVG, BVI, Shaker/Converted, African-derived Caribbean religion, Akan tradition, and Christianity — personal number symbolism kept explicitly separate from historical evidence
    • Animals and animal symbolism: birds, snakes, frogs, insects, butterflies/moths, sea creatures — which were food, medicine, omens, messengers, feared — with no assumption of one universal African meaning across contexts
    • Food as medicine, ritual, and identity: cornmeal, okra, cassava, provision grounds, bush teas, fasting, ritual meals, food given to the dead, pregnancy/postpartum/children's foods
    • Astronomy: moon, stars, eclipses, navigation, agricultural timing, maritime knowledge, celestial omens

    🌑 SHADOW

    • (Folds together with POWER above — death, danger, poisoning, spiritual harm as their own honest field of study, not avoided out of squeamishness, but never turned into an operational how-to)

    🔒 SECRECY

    • Coded transmission: euphemism, Christian cover language, songs, proverbs, food, household customs, seemingly ordinary practices as vehicles for hidden knowledge. Ask not just "where is the Obeah ritual" but "could something have survived because nobody called it Obeah?"
    • Fraud and spiritual exploitation, studied historically: fraudulent healers, financial exploitation, fear-based services, fabricated curses, coercive spiritual authority — discernment isn't only recognizing a spirit, it's recognizing manipulation

    📜 HISTORY

    • Colonial suppression and criminalization as a full pillar: Obeah laws, Shaker prohibitions, missionary suppression, prosecutions, confiscation of objects, forced Christianization, how practitioners changed vocabulary to survive
    • Politics and resistance: Obeah's relationship to slavery, rebellion, maroonage, labor disputes, colonial surveillance, and how accusation itself became a tool of control
    • Migration as cultural transmission, tracked concretely: person → boat → port → village → marriage → church → occupation → household → child → practice
    • Economics and spiritual power: money, healers' fees, gift exchange, reciprocity, land, inheritance — spiritual authority doesn't exist outside society
    • Christianity as part of the system, not automatically its opposite: Christianity ↔ Shakers ↔ Spiritual Baptists/Converted ↔ African-derived knowledge, asking what African-derived structures survived while people spoke explicitly Christian language
    • Indigenous Caribbean knowledge held as its own thread, not swallowed by the African component: Kalinago/Carib history, Taíno/Arawakan influences, Indigenous plants and material culture, Afro-Indigenous exchange
    • European folk practices as a possible third source alongside African and Indigenous ones — British folk belief, maritime superstition, European herbal medicine, colonial household custom

    🧭 DISCERNMENT

    • The psychology of belief, held beside spirituality rather than replacing it: placebo/nocebo, expectation, grief, suggestion, trauma, pattern recognition, confirmation bias. A serious practitioner holds both explanations without collapsing one into the other
    • Comparative diaspora methodology: Akan ≠ Igbo ≠ Kongo ≠ Yoruba ≠ Indigenous Caribbean ≠ Vincentian Shaker ≠ BVI fungi culture — comparison identifies recurring structures without collapsing distinct traditions into one another. The trap to avoid: "people in Africa do X, therefore my Caribbean ancestors did X"
    • Language as its own serious branch: Akan/Twi, Igbo, African linguistic retention, Vincentian and BVI Creole, plant/spiritual/place-name vocabulary — every proposed African etymology tagged documented / proposed / disputed / unsupported
    • Research methodology itself: archives, paleography, genealogy, ethnography, oral history method, botanical identification, historical linguistics, archaeology, source criticism, colonial terminology, church/cemetery/court/shipping/estate/census records

    🌱 PRACTICE — the Bush Girl Field Journal

    • Separate from the research document. Every plant, dream, recurring symbol, family custom remembered, coincidence, spiritual experience, piece of folklore, song, prayer, bodily sensation, place, or death/mourning custom encountered gets written down — labeled PERS (personal experience), not automatically ANCESTRAL. That distinction protects the practice from becoming fantasy while still letting mystery remain mystery.

    🧬 The Akan Hypothesis

    Held as an active hypothesis with labeled confidence levels, not a conclusion.

    • ESTABLISHED Akan people were among Africans brought to Tortola
    • ESTABLISHED Igbo populations were also significant there
    • ESTABLISHED Virgin Islands cultural terms such as fungi and camfou/comfoo have proposed (not confirmed) African linguistic connections
    • UNRESOLVED which traditions survived specifically through Akan-descended Tortolans
    • UNRESOLVED whether the maternal Vincentian line descends from Akan populations
    • UNRESOLVED whether particular family practices have Akan ancestry specifically
    • PERSONAL a strong spiritual/intellectual resonance with Akan cosmology — allowed to exist as its own category, without needing to become genealogy

    ⚖️ Comparative Framework — Obeah / Shaker / Christianity / Akan

    A research tool, not a claim that all practitioners within any one tradition believe identically. Compare across: main concern, divination, healing, plants, dreams, ancestors, spirit possession/trance, and colonial suppression — for each tradition — before assuming resemblance means shared origin.

    The 2024 Oxford Handbook of Caribbean Religions treats divination, healing, protection, possession, and Obeah as related but distinct Caribbean phenomena, emphasizing their mobility and variation — a genuinely useful framework text for this comparison.

    🩹 Bush Girl Ethics

    • I do not claim ancestry I cannot establish.
    • I do not call every African-derived practice Obeah.
    • I do not call every herbal remedy safe because it is traditional.
    • I distinguish historical evidence from personal revelation.
    • I do not reproduce sacred practices simply because I found them in a book.
    • I respect living practitioners as knowledge holders.
    • I don't expose restricted knowledge for proof.
    • I document plants carefully.
    • I learn when not to use a plant.
    • I don't replace medical care with spiritual work.
    • I don't exploit vulnerable people who come to me for healing.
    • I protect people's privacy.
    • I don't turn my ancestors into aesthetic props.
    • I allow unanswered questions to remain unanswered.

    🚩 Do Not Learn This From TikTok — Red Flags

    • "All African spirituality is the same."
    • "Obeah is basically Caribbean witchcraft."
    • "If you feel it, you’re definitely descended from X."
    • "This word sounds African, therefore it came from X."
    • "This herb cures everything."
    • "Ancestors told me this is your lineage."
    • "Pay me and I’ll activate your bloodline."
    • "You need initiation immediately."
    • "Everyone who disagrees is spiritually attacked."

    Skepticism here is not a rejection of spirituality. It's part of the spiritual discipline.

    📚 Reading List for This Roadmap — Verified

    • VERIFIED Adrian Fraser — From Shakers to Spiritual Baptists: The Struggle for Survival of the Shakers of St. Vincent and the Grenadines (2012) — real Vincentian historian (PhD, University of Western Ontario; also authored a biography of Chatoyer, SVG's national hero); traces the 1912 Shaker Prohibition Ordinance and the fight to repeal it, centered on the 1935 riots
    • VERIFIED J. Brent Crosson — Experiments with Power: Obeah and the Remaking of Religion in Trinidad (University of Chicago Press) — real, based on 11 years of ethnographic fieldwork; structured around the three movements of Spiritual Baptist mourning specifically; examines Obeah as a justice-making practice tied to real 2011 Trinidad police violence cases
    • Patricia Stephens — The Spiritual Baptist Faith — already logged in the main Root Below the Root document
    • Diana Paton & Maarit Forde, eds. — Obeah and Other Powers — already owned/on order

    Not independently re-verified this round — worth checking before buying: Cecilia Sem Obeng's two books on Akan traditional healing (Traditional Healing Practices Among the Asuom People of Ghana; Voices of Affliction), and Lauren Coyle Rosen — Law in Light. All three are plausible and specific enough to likely be real, but weren't run through the same verification process as the two above.

    🧭 Practitioner Formation & Judgment

    Not a seventh subject — a layer of discernment that runs across every branch above. Knowledge and judgment are different skills; this section trains the second one.

    The Discernment Chain

    Before interpreting anything spiritually, work this in order. Skipping a step is exactly the habit this framework exists to prevent.

    1. Observation — what is actually happening, described without interpretation
    2. Ordinary possibilities — medical, psychological, social, environmental, coincidental explanations
    3. Spiritual possibilities — named specifically per the relevant tradition, not generically
    4. Evidence — what would distinguish the ordinary explanation from the spiritual one
    5. Urgency — safe to sit with, or needs immediate action
    6. Consent — has the person asked for involvement, on what terms
    7. Response — what's safe to offer given everything above
    8. Referral/Wait — belongs with another professional, or simply needs time
    9. Follow-up — what gets checked on, and when

    When Not to Work

    Not every problem needs a ritual, an ancestor, an herb, or divination.

    STOP → OBSERVE → REFER → WAIT → WORK, in that order

    • STOP applies to: medical emergencies, psychiatric crisis, coercion, domestic danger, anything not understood
    • WAIT is a legitimate answer — not every situation resolves faster because of action taken

    Case-Study Method

    Work all ten questions before any action: what's known / what's only interpretation / mundane explanations / plausible spiritual interpretations / distinguishing evidence / what should NOT be done / what's safe to recommend / when to refer / what would confirm / what would disconfirm.

    Worked example (nightmares, exhaustion, family conflict, objects moving, believed spiritual attack): the exercise deliberately does not produce a ritual — it holds the question open long enough to actually investigate, applied under real-time pressure rather than at leisure.

    Failure Analysis

    Study how a practitioner can be wrong, not only how the work is supposed to work.

    Confirmation biasFear creating interpretationCoincidence read as causationProjectionPractitioner egoWishful thinkingCommunity pressureMisrememberingFalse attributionConfusing correlation with spiritual causationTreating every dream as instructionAssuming an outcome proves the ritual caused it

    Practitioner Ethics — Addendum to Bush Girl Ethics

    • I diagnose slowly; a spiritual explanation is earned through investigation, not assumed first
    • I do not treat every disagreement, coincidence, or unexplained event as confirmation
    • I refer out for anything medical, psychiatric, or in crisis
    • I do not name a person as the source of an affliction without evidence
    • I hold my own claims of authority to the same standard I'd hold someone else's
    • I record failures and ambiguous cases as carefully as successes
    • I practice attention, patience, emotional control, secrecy, and humility — and watch my own ego
    • I know the most disciplined thing I can do, some of the time, is nothing

    Apprenticeship, Authority & Transmission

    Being historically knowledgeable isn't automatically the same as being a practitioner.

    Apprenticeship and formation
    Elder/teacher relationships; initiation vs. education (learned by permission vs. by reading); restricted knowledge that should never be self-taught; how communities recognize competence
    How knowledge actually travels
    Relevant to the lineage question too: mother→child, grandmother→grandchild, woman→woman, neighbor→child, church→household, marriage, migration, maritime travel, markets, food, music, language, nicknames, funerals, domestic habits

    Ritual Theory

    Not another list of rituals — the shared architecture underneath them. Ask the same questions of Obeah, Shaker/Converted, Akan, Jamaican Myal, Revival, and family practice, side by side: sequence, preparation, threshold/space, time, repetition, words, silence, body, voice, movement, objects, water, fire, plants, food, clothing, music/sound/rhythm, witnesses, ancestors/spirits, closure, aftermath.

    Practitioner Log — Separate from the Field Journal

    The Field Journal records what happened. This records what was decided, and why: date, situation, who was involved, what was reported vs. observed, ordinary and spiritual explanations considered, evidence level, action taken and why, consent, safety concerns, outcome, what's still unknown.

    Oath Addendum

    “I do not mistake knowing for knowing what to do. I hold the question open before I hold a conclusion. I let a wrong guess be a wrong guess, not a hidden one. I send people to the help they need, even when it isn't me. Judgment is a practice, the same as any other — and I return to it, case by case.”

    📚 Practitioner Research Library — New Sources

    Organized by evidentiary circle, so ancestry, historical evidence, and comparative study don't blur together. Circle 1: direct Vincentian. Circle 2: Tortolan. Circle 3: Jamaican comparative. Circle 4: broader Caribbean formation.

    • Marie Meudec — "Ordinary Ethics of Spiritual Work and Healing in St. Lucia" (Small Axe, 2017) — St. Lucian spiritual workers often don’t identify their own practice with the label "Obeah"; a real caution against deciding for practitioners what their practice is called
    • Steve Weaver — ethnographic methods study of Obeah practitioners, St. Thomas, Jamaica — how the researcher gained access to a marginalized practitioner community; directly useful for apprenticeship/trust/boundary questions
    • The Mammy Forbes case (Rose Ann "Mammy" Forbes) — a Jamaican balmyard operator whose practice began with a healing vision; husband and daughter continued the work; encountered legal prosecution. A complete practitioner-life arc: calling → healing → community → family transmission → reputation → legal pressure → succession
    • DIRECT SVG CONNECTION Daniel Young — an SVG migrant prosecuted for Obeah in Trinidad, 1931 (Obeah Histories case database) — a real named case tying St. Vincent specifically to the historical Obeah court record
    • Additional named court cases for case-study practice: Polydore (Jamaica, 1831), Pierre (Grenada), Charles Dolly (Montserrat), Rose Ann/George Forbes (Jamaica), Cindy Brooks (Jamaica, 1964)
    • Myal Jamaica (community resource) — contemporary practitioner/community FAQ on Myal's relationship to what outsiders call Obeah; used as living community testimony compared against academic sources, not primary historical authority

    🌍 Comparative Material — Folded In From Broader Research

    From the Ancient Technologies and Worlds Behind the World archives — real, but comparative-only unless marked otherwise. Held here rather than as separate standalone files.

    Body & Healing (Comparative)

    • Kisii skull surgery/omobari omotwe (Kenya) — documented trepanation with herbal pain management; East African, comparative only — the transatlantic trade reaching Jamaica/SVG/Tortola drew from West/Central Africa, not East Africa
    • Bone-setting traditions documented among Yoruba and Ewe practitioners — whether a specific Caribbean lineage survived in Jamaica, St. Vincent, or Tortola hasn't been investigated yet; Jamaica is the most promising starting point
    • Cassava detoxification as applied chemistry — grating, pressing, washing, fermenting, heating to remove cyanogenic compounds; Indigenous Caribbean/South American in origin
    • Kalle Kananoja — Healing Knowledge in Atlantic Africa — medical specialists and therapeutic knowledge in the actual African regions Caribbean populations were taken from; connections traced practice-by-practice, not assumed wholesale

    Death, Dreams & Transformation (Comparative)

    • Wade Davis — Passage of Darkness / The Serpent and the Rainbow — Haitian zombification investigated anthropologically; the pharmacological explanation remains heavily debated
    • Philippe Charlier — Zombies: An Anthropological Investigation of the Living Dead — distinguishes corporeal zombie, spiritual/astral zombie, social death, and loss of free will
    • Todd Ramón Ochoa — Society of the Dead: Quita Manaquita and Palo Praise in Cuba — a Kongo-inspired world where the dead, events, and materials are deeply interconnected; comparative Kongo depth, not evidence of Vincentian/Jamaican/Tortolan ancestry
    • Adam McGee — scholarship on dreaming in Haitian Vodou as a source of guidance and religious innovation — comparative model for dream-instruction elsewhere in the diaspora

    Research rule for the zombie/zonbi branch specifically: never start with movies. Start with Haitian history, then Vodou cosmology, then Haitian concepts of personhood, then the zonbi scholarship itself.

    🎯 How to Actually Use This Document

    Not sequentially. Not as homework. When something from the active reading — Creole Religions, Caribbean Religious History, Obeah and Other Powers, or whatever comes next — naturally opens a question that belongs to one of these 16 branches, that's the moment to come back here, not before. This document waits. It doesn't pull.

    The Living Library & The Bush Oracle

    An Expanded Curriculum for Interdisciplinary Mastery, Ancestral Knowledge, Creative Sovereignty & Practical Skill

    With weekly lesson plans

    I. The Purpose of This Curriculum

    The purpose of this curriculum is to develop a person who can study deeply, understand systems, recognise relationships between disciplines, preserve knowledge, create tangible things, and apply what they learn.

    The goal is not to collect hobbies or become superficially familiar with many subjects. The goal is to develop interconnected forms of knowledge until they become usable skills, creative abilities, and bodies of work.

    The Living Library is an evolving personal institution: a place where knowledge is studied, experienced, questioned, documented, practised, preserved, and eventually transformed into something that can be shared or built upon.

    The Bush Oracle is the living relationship between observation, intuition, ancestry, land, sound, memory, creativity, and interpretation. It is not limited to one academic discipline. It develops through the study of the natural world, cultural traditions, the body, historical knowledge, artistic expression, and the ability to recognise connections.

    The curriculum should cultivate

    • Intellectual mastery: understanding how systems work, how knowledge is produced, and how different disciplines connect.
    • Practical mastery: developing the ability to make, repair, grow, formulate, design, build, and experiment.
    • Cultural and ancestral literacy: researching Caribbean histories, traditions, technologies, ecological knowledge, language, and artistic practices with attention to their specific communities.
    • Creative mastery: turning knowledge into music, writing, visual art, physical objects, digital experiences, and original systems.
    • Spiritual and reflective development: preserving dreams, downloads, personal interpretations, embodied experiences, and spiritual understandings as part of the evolving archive.
    • Digital sovereignty: learning to build, maintain, and control the digital environments through which knowledge is organised and shared.
    • Self-sufficiency: developing the ability to solve problems, learn independently, and create with accessible resources.

    The ultimate objective is not to know everything. It is to become increasingly capable of learning almost anything, understanding how it relates to other things, and applying that understanding.

    II. The Original Twelve Branches Remain the Foundation

    The twelve branches already established in the original Life Purpose blueprint remain the primary structure of the curriculum: the Earthkeeper, the Alchemist, the Apothecary, the Hearthkeeper, the Soundkeeper, the Adornment Architect, the Archivist, the Oracle, the Architect, the Elementalist, the Strategist and the Storyteller.

    This expansion is not a replacement taxonomy. New disciplines, crafts, sciences, technologies, and research methods should be incorporated into the existing branches wherever they naturally belong.

    A subject may serve more than one branch. For example, sound can be studied through physics, music, cultural history, spirituality, mathematics, and material construction. Botany can connect to ecology, medicine history, chemistry, agriculture, dyeing, foodways, and ancestral knowledge.

    The branches should therefore function as interconnected fields rather than isolated boxes.

    Curriculum rule: preserve the original branch names, descriptions, purposes, and existing content. Add new disciplines beneath or alongside them without removing their original meaning.

    III. Seven Interconnected Mastery Worlds

    The following seven worlds are an additional organising layer for the new disciplines. They are not replacements for the twelve original branches. They are a way of grouping the subjects that will help develop them.

    1 The Earthkeeper: Land, Ecology & Living Systems

    The study of the Earth as a living system, including its materials, cycles, organisms, landscapes, and relationships with human communities.

    Disciplines to explore

    • Botany and plant taxonomy
    • Ethnobotany and traditional ecological knowledge
    • Soil science and pedology
    • Agroecology and permaculture
    • Agroforestry and food forests
    • Hydrology and watershed systems
    • Geology and mineralogy
    • Mycology and fungi
    • Ecology and biodiversity
    • Environmental science
    • Seed saving and plant propagation
    • Composting and soil regeneration
    • Ethnoastronomy and relationships between land, sky, and seasonal cycles

    Caribbean and place-based directions

    • Caribbean flora and plant identification
    • St. Vincent and the Grenadines' ecosystems
    • Tortola and the wider Virgin Islands' ecology
    • Traditional food crops and agricultural practices
    • Bush knowledge and community-specific plant traditions
    • Rainfall, drought, watersheds, coastal environments, and island geology
    • Traditional ecological knowledge and the relationship between people and land

    Practical abilities to develop

    Identify plants, understand soil, observe ecosystems, grow food, propagate plants, recognise environmental changes, document local biodiversity, and understand how land supports human life.

    2 The Alchemist: Chemistry, Transformation & Formulation

    The study of how materials change, how substances interact, and how natural and manufactured materials can be transformed into useful products.

    Disciplines to explore

    • General chemistry
    • Organic chemistry
    • Biochemistry
    • Phytochemistry
    • Acid–base chemistry
    • Material chemistry
    • Natural pigments and dyes
    • Extraction and separation techniques
    • Fermentation science
    • Food chemistry
    • Cosmetic chemistry and formulation
    • Soapmaking and surfactant chemistry
    • Textile chemistry
    • Mordants and dye fixation
    • Ethnobotanical extraction and historical preparation methods

    Specific craft and science directions

    • Indigo vat dyeing and the chemistry of indigo reduction and oxidation
    • Plant-based dyes and mordants
    • Anthocyanin pigment extraction
    • Natural ink and pigment preparation
    • Tincture and infusion theory, with careful separation of historical practice from medical claims
    • Food preservation and fermentation
    • Material testing and colourfastness

    Practical abilities to develop

    Understand solutions, mixtures, pH, solubility, extraction, concentration, pigments, emulsions, and material reactions. Learn how to document experiments, control variables, compare results, and formulate simple products safely.

    The Alchemist should develop an understanding of both the scientific principles and the cultural histories of transformation.

    3 The Architect: Structures, Materials & Mechanical Systems

    The study of how things are designed, constructed, joined, shaped, and made to function.

    Disciplines to explore

    • Mechanical engineering
    • Structural engineering fundamentals
    • Materials science
    • Woodworking and joinery

    • Hollow-body construction and resonant cavities
    • Soundboard and instrument-body construction
    • Traditional joinery and furniture-making
    • Dry-stone wall principles
    • Earth-wall construction and material selection
    • Calabash craft and natural-object construction
    • Basketry, weaving, and traditional cordage

    Practical abilities to develop

    Understand forces, load, balance, tension, compression, material properties, joints, structural forms, tolerances, and construction sequences.

    Advanced construction should follow appropriate instruction, supervision, tools, and safety requirements. The beginner stage should focus on understanding, drawings, small models, and safe material experiments.

    4 The Soundkeeper: Sound, Music & Vibration

    The study of sound as a physical phenomenon, an artistic medium, a cultural technology, and a form of communication.

    Disciplines to explore

    • Acoustics
    • Psychoacoustics
    • Vibration physics
    • Sound engineering
    • Audio production
    • Music theory
    • Ethnomusicology
    • Instrument design
    • Resonance and harmonic systems
    • Sound recording
    • Signal processing
    • Electronics for audio
    • Room acoustics
    • Rhythm and polyrhythm
    • Vocal production
    • Historical sound technologies
    • Caribbean musical traditions

    Specific directions

    • Acoustic resonator craft
    • Soundboard construction and material behaviour
    • Resonance chambers and hollow-body instruments
    • Building simple acoustic experiments
    • Understanding the relationship between shape, material, and tone
    • Studying Caribbean percussion, rhythm, call-and-response, and musical transmission
    • Developing audio engineering and production skills
    • Connecting sound research to original music-making

    Practical abilities to develop

    Understand frequency, amplitude, resonance, timbre, harmonics, waveforms, reverberation, phase, rhythm, and the interaction between materials and sound.

    This world should connect physical acoustics with cultural research and personal musical practice without assuming that all Caribbean sound traditions share the same origins or meanings.

    5 The Oracle: Observation, Interpretation & Systems of Meaning

    The study of perception, symbolic systems, philosophy, the natural world, the sky, memory, and the ways people interpret experience.

    Disciplines to explore

    • Mathematics and pattern recognition
    • Systems thinking
    • Logic and critical reasoning

    Practical abilities to develop

    Observe carefully, identify patterns, distinguish observations from interpretations, understand symbolic frameworks, compare different explanations, and develop a personal record of recurring ideas and experiences.

    The Oracle's work should preserve spiritual and intuitive interpretations as their own category of knowledge. They should not be erased simply because they are not academic claims. At the same time, historical, scientific, cultural, and personal interpretations should remain distinguishable so the archive can retain its integrity.

    Practical abilities to develop

    Locate and evaluate sources, record oral histories, organise research, trace terminology, compare historical accounts, preserve documents, build bibliographies, and maintain a clear record of where information came from.

    Research should preserve distinctions between documented historical evidence, community testimony, family memory, personal experience, and spiritual interpretation.

    The digital sanctuary

    The website for the research project should become a practical learning environment and an evolving digital home for the Living Library. The long-term goal is to develop the ability to:

    • Build and maintain original websites and applications.
    • Understand the code behind the interfaces rather than depending entirely on AI-generated prototypes.
    • Create interactive research archives.
    • Design astrology and almanac interfaces.
    • Build interactive cards, calendars, transit calculators, and tabbed reference systems.
    • Organise documents, images, research notes, and multimedia.
    • Develop a distinctive visual language using dark celestial, aged star-chart, botanical, and archival aesthetics.
    • Preserve digital artefacts and maintain control over the project's structure and presentation.
    • Eventually create independent digital products and tools.

    The website is not separate from the curriculum. It is where the knowledge can be organised, tested, presented, and made useful.

    Integration module: web development & digital artefact curation

    • Core objective: use self-taught front-end coding (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) to independently build, style, and deploy web applications and digital interfaces, moving from AI-assisted prototyping to hands-on code ownership.
    • The digital medium as sanctuary: translating sovereign spiritual systems, customised astrology and almanac interfaces (such as the Co–Star hybrid daily oracle), and personal archives into functional, highly curated web experiences.
    • Aesthetic and technical standards: dark, atmospheric, celestial and high-craft UI design; strict typography, custom layouts, and interactive components (for example dynamic "Do and Don't" card draws, personalised transit calculators, and tabbed almanacs); tools that feel hand-crafted rather than mass-market or sterile.
    • Long-term market and sovereignty vision: packaging and marketing custom, value-driven web applications and digital products as premium, independent assets, keeping complete creative control and the technical infrastructure self-sustained behind the veil.
